question: Why is the bitter taste sense important for humans from a survival standpoint?

options.A: Detecting potential poisons and harmful alkaloids
options.B: Signaling the presence of dietary carbohydrates
options.C: Regulating cellular sodium and electrolyte balance
options.D: Identifying protein-rich amino acids in food

explanation: Bitter taste receptors evolved to protect the body by warning against eating toxic compounds. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h1)

question: What makes the full experience of food flavor different from just basic taste?

options.A: Exclusively relying on salivary gland enzyme activity
options.B: Activation of only salt and sweet receptor cells
options.C: Processing solely within the primary somatosensory cortex
options.D: Integration of olfactory, textural, and thermal inputs

explanation: True flavor perception requires the brain to combine taste signals with smell, texture, and temperature. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h1)

question: Which type of tongue papillae does not contain any taste buds?
explanation: Filiform papillae cover the tongue to provide texture and friction, but they do not have taste buds. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h2)

question: Where are circumvallate papillae usually found on the tongue?

options.B: Scattered evenly across the tip of the tongue
options.C: Along the anterior two-thirds of the surface
options.D: In a V-shape at the posterior region

explanation: Circumvallate papillae form a clear V-shaped row near the back of the tongue. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h2)

question: What is the main job of Type IV taste bud cells?

options.A: Expressing G-protein coupled receptors for bitter compounds
options.B: Forming conventional chemical synapses with afferent nerves
options.C: Serving as supporting glial-like cells that clear neurotransmitters
options.D: Acting as stem cells to replace older receptor cells

explanation: Type IV basal cells divide and develop into new taste receptor cells to replace older ones. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h3)

question: Which taste cell type makes direct chemical connections with sensory nerve fibers?
explanation: Type III cells contain special vesicles that form true chemical synapses with nerve endings. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h3)

question: Which ion is mainly responsible for making food taste salty?
explanation: Sodium ions enter through channels on the cell surface to directly trigger a salty taste response. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h4)

question: How do hydrogen ions mainly start the sour taste process in receptor cells?

options.A: By entering through specific proton channels to depolarize the cell
options.B: By activating cyclic adenosine monophosphate second messengers
options.C: By inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels on nerve endings
options.D: By binding directly to intracellular G-protein coupled receptors

explanation: Protons from acids flow straight into Type III cells, causing an electrical shift that triggers signaling. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h4)

question: Which pair of receptor proteins creates the working umami taste receptor?
explanation: The T1R1 and T1R3 proteins link together to recognize amino acids like glutamate, creating the umami taste. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h5)

question: Which molecule inside the cell directly triggers the release of calcium during sweet taste processing?
explanation: Activating phospholipase C produces inositol trisphosphate, which causes calcium to be released from internal storage. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h5)

question: Which cranial nerve carries taste signals from the front two-thirds of the tongue?
explanation: The facial nerve, via its chorda tympani branch, supplies sensory fibers to the front part of the tongue. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h6)

question: Where do taste nerve fibers make their very first stop in the central nervous system?
explanation: All primary taste nerve fibers synapse first in the nucleus of the solitary tract located in the medulla. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h6)

question: Where in the human brain is the primary gustatory cortex found?

options.B: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
options.C: Temporal lobe inferior to the hippocampus
options.D: Occipital lobe near the visual cortex

explanation: Conscious awareness of taste happens mainly in the anterior insular cortex and frontal operculum. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h7)

question: What is an important result when taste signals reach the hypothalamus?

options.A: Long-term storage of declarative memories regarding food names
options.B: Regulation of autonomic responses like digestion and satiety
options.C: Direct motor control of tongue muscles during active chewing
options.D: Initial conversion of volatile odorants into electrical impulses

explanation: Connections to the hypothalamus link taste information with body needs, eating habits, and automatic body responses. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T10#GNS211_U4_T10_h7)
